source_terms: The only way to come close to this in a still image is to arrange the framing, composition or lighting so that all the attention immediately goes to one place, but the eye lingers long enough on the frame to start to wander, and then discovers something else.

It’s an uncertain balancing act, because if you hide the thing-to-be-revealed too well, such as by making it too small or poorly lit, chances are the viewer will get bored and move on before noticing it.
item.claim: The reveal is a cinematic device — the camera shows one thing, then moves or zooms to disclose something else, effective through surprise — and the source says it is difficult and perhaps impossible to achieve in a single still. The only approach is to arrange framing, composition or lighting so that attention goes immediately to one place, but the eye lingers long enough to start wandering and then discovers something else. It is an uncertain balancing act: hide the thing to be revealed too well — too small, too poorly lit — and the viewer will get bored and move on before noticing it.

mechanism.text: In film the disclosure is controlled by the camera's movement. In a still it must be produced by the viewer's own scanning, so the photographer controls only how long the first subject holds and how findable the second is.

scope.conditions: a still image with a secondary subject intended to be found late

item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', section 'Complex Surfaces', the closing figure
item.question: The book says adding a three-dimensional object to a glossy flat surface both improves the picture and makes the lighting easier. Why does it help, and why does the chapter drop the idea immediately?
item.answer: It helps because the object's reflection in the surface is unambiguous evidence of gloss in a way that a featureless bright area is not: the reflection of a pair of eyeglasses in a polished lid tells the viewer the wood is glossy, and the authors say adding a secondary subject reveals the surface better than they are likely to render it alone. It makes the lighting easier for the same reason — the proof of the finish no longer has to be carried entirely by the shaped highlight. The chapter drops it because it had committed at the outset to two-dimensional and nearly two-dimensional subjects, and the authors say they cannot pursue the approach far without breaking that promise; three-dimensional subjects are the next chapter's business. So the claim is stated and demonstrated but deliberately not developed.

assuming the book recommends it generally; it raises it and sets it aside for structural reasons

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Secondary Opaque Subjects'
item.question: A labelled glass bottle has to look premium and its label has to be legible. The lighting that gives the bottle its describing highlight puts a sheen across the paper. Work through the book's options and say which it rules out and why.
item.answer: The conflict is real and the book states it: most of a paper's reflection is diffuse but some is direct, so the light producing the direct reflection on the glass is also likely to obscure the label. Two remedies work. Move the offending light higher, so the label's direct reflection goes downward instead of toward the lens. Or, where good highlight placement forbids moving the light, interpose a small opaque card blocking exactly the angles that produce direct reflection on the label — and its size is critical: a gobo extending beyond the label's own family of angles will itself reflect in the glass. A polarizing filter is the third option and the book rules it out in most cases: much of the desirable highlight on the glass is usually polarized already, so a polarizer that eliminates the label's reflection is also likely to interfere with the light the glass needs. Underneath all three sits the prior question the authors insist comes first — which of the two is the principal subject — and they say that cannot be settled on a technical basis at all.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'Secondary Opaque Subjects' for the three options and the gobo size constraint; 'Recognizing the Principal Subject' for the prior decision.
confounders: reaching for the polarizer first, which is the intuitive move and the one the source blocks here
oversizing the gobo, which converts a label fix into a black reflection in the glass
treating this as a legibility defect rather than as a scene lit for the wrong principal subject

source_terms: Framing the shot usually comes before anything else—the first decision.

Composition (or design if you like) covers the whole range of organizing the image, while framing concentrates on enclosing the scene, even before thinking about the relationship between elements inside the picture.
item.claim: Framing and composition are different acts. Framing concentrates on enclosing the scene and comes before anything else, prior even to thinking about relationships between the elements inside the picture; composition covers the whole range of organising the image. The source notes the term comes from filmmaking, where a scene is enclosed and the action then plays out within it, and concedes the separation is less sharp in still photography, where the image is singular rather than multiple. Even so, the decisions about where to cut into a landscape, figure or object, and what to include and leave out, rank as the most important in defining the shot.

mechanism.text: In film the enclosure is fixed first and the action happens inside it, which is what makes framing logically prior. The source imports that ordering into still photography while acknowledging it fits less cleanly.

caveats.text: the source states directly that the separation may not hold to the same degree in still photography
the claim that framing decisions are the most important in defining the shot is asserted and is not revisited or tested anywhere in the three parts

item.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
item.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the aestheticisation passages (spine 8), against "In Plato's Cave", the passage on moral position (spine 5)
item.question: Someone cites Sontag to argue that a particular photograph should have been composed differently so as not to aestheticise its subject. Is that a use of her argument? Answer from the text.
item.answer: No, and the reason is in the shape of the claim rather than in a matter of taste. Her claim is that photography still beautifies notwithstanding the declared aims of harsh, unposed photography to reveal truth and not beauty, and that this holds for the most well-intentioned and properly captioned work. A tendency that survives the intention to defeat it, and survives accurate captioning, is not one a different composition escapes — so the claim cannot ground a recommendation about composing. She also nowhere recommends anything: she describes what the medium does to a viewer's relation to a subject and stops. Her related claim about what images can accomplish runs the same way — photographs reinforce a moral position and do not create one, which is a statement about what determines an image's effect, not a specification for making one. Using her to prescribe a composition attributes to her a kind of statement she does not make anywhere in the book.
item.support: The Heroism of Vision: notwithstanding the declared aims of indiscreet, unposed, often harsh photography to reveal truth, not beauty, photography still beautifies; in a consumer society, even the most well-intentioned and properly captioned work issues in the discovery of beauty. In Plato's Cave: photographs cannot create a moral position, but they can reinforce one.
confounders: reading the aestheticisation claim as an instruction, which is the standard misuse of this source
assuming that because she disapproves of an effect she must be recommending against a technique
concluding instead that she thinks such images should not be made; she says nothing of the kind

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: What contrast does the source draw between Indian and contemporary Western posters, and what reason does it give for the Indian side of it?
item.answer: Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which the public must see the film to resolve, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as 'the media seal of approval' plus studio, producer and director credits signalling the film's status. Indian posters 'rarely use text'. The reason given is distribution: with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier' — text picks a language, and picking a language cuts the audience. From the 1980s it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are themselves a marker of the style, content and quality of the film.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: The absence of text is not an aesthetic preference in this account; it is a response to a multilingual distribution constraint, and the three names that DO appear are doing the work the review quotations do elsewhere.

source_terms: it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer
item.claim: Bijapurkar identifies a specific misdiagnosis and corrects it. When richer consumers began buying popular-segment rather than premium products, marketers called this "down-trading" and "many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy." Her correction: "In fact, it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer and the popular and discount segments, in many cases, now offer a real value advantage in terms of equivalent if not better benefits at a lower price." She supplies the supply-side cause: unequal tax and duty incentives were withdrawn, forcing small manufacturers into open competition, which produced "rogue" marketers who refused to respect the unwritten price-performance rules, so consumers faced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. She gives the automotive instances — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B- segment car with premium features — and concludes that "the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant."

mechanism.text: Observed behaviour changed because the choice set changed, not because preferences did. When the price-performance frontier moves, a buyer whose preferences are unchanged will appear at a different point on the old segmentation — and an analyst who holds the segmentation fixed will attribute the movement to the buyer's character.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets after the withdrawal of differential tax and duty structures, principally FMCG, automotive, PCs and industrial water treatment, over roughly 1991-2009.

caveats.text: THE GENERAL SHAPE IS THE VALUABLE PART AND IT IS NOT INDIAN. Attributing a shift in observed behaviour to consumer character when the choice set moved is a reasoning error available anywhere. The specific instances are dated
the cases are named products and are checkable in principle, but no market-share, price or volume data is given for any of them

the author also offers a second, different explanation elsewhere for the same FMCG stagnation — a 'change confluence' in which consumer credit and durables purchases committed future income, forcing careful FMCG spending. The two explanations are compatible but are not reconciled, and the book presents each as sufficient in its own place

source_terms: each distinct phase in development marked a distinct aesthetic change in advertising
item.claim: Patel's organising claim for chapter 3 is that Indian film advertising did not evolve toward a single style but moved through distinct phases, each borrowing "the aesthetic vocabulary of the period." She sets out the sequence: text-only newspaper notices and handbills (1896 onward); the Ravi Varma aesthetic, realist oil technique applied to Hindu mythological subject matter, carried into posters via the Varma press's oleographs; the Bombay School of Art style, a delicate realism tied to Ajanta revival and used when a studio wanted to signal that a film was special; Art Deco from the 1930s as a universal symbol of modernity, which "did not survive beyond the end of the 1940s" in India because it was seen as Western cultural imperialism; nationalist imagery around Independence, often using the map of India; overpainted montage in the 1970s-80s; and computer-aided design from the 1990s.

mechanism.text: Patel's stated mechanism is that a style already carries associations before a poster uses it, so choosing a style is a way of saying something the image itself does not have to depict. She states it explicitly for the art-school style: it was "referred to whenever there was a need to communicate more than the basic information about a film," and in these instances "the mode of representation was often used to reflect or reinforce underlying messages about current cultural and political issues."

scope.conditions: Indian film advertising 1896-2002. Every phase is dated by the source. The claim is a periodisation, not a description of a standing style.

caveats.text: THIS IS THE OBJECT THAT PROTECTS THE REST FROM BEING FLATTENED. The source's own thesis is that the style changed repeatedly and that each change tracked a change in its environment. Any use of this book that produces a single timeless 'Indian poster style' contradicts the source's central argument
the mechanism — style carries prior association — is stated and illustrated but not tested; the source shows that designers used styles this way, not that audiences read them so
attributions are uneven: many booklets and posters of the period 'were unsigned', and Patel says so. Some phase-to-artist assignments therefore rest on stylistic attribution

item.question: What changed about who wrote Indian advertising from the mid-1970s, and what is the precise distinction the source draws?
item.answer: Through the 1960s and 70s the business was dominated by English-medium, convent-educated writers who had succeeded the departing British admen, and Indian-language writers were confined to a separate 'Language Department'. From the mid-1970s writers such as Kamlesh Pandey began creating work ORIGINALLY in Hindi rather than translating into it, and the source names Piyush Pandey, Balki and Prasoon Joshi as continuing that. The precise distinction is origination versus translation — the source draws it explicitly, saying the work was 'all originally created in Hindi' — and it matters because confining a language to a translation function separates the language from the idea.
item.support: 'Indian language writers were confined to the "Language Department"… all originally created in Hindi'
item.confounders: An insider's history told through individuals he knew; no institutional data on department structure or staffing is offered.

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Verbal and Editorial Deconstruction (spine 6)
item.question: You are laying out a transcript of a heated argument between three speakers. Using Samara's verbal deconstruction, what is the source of the layout's structure, and what specifically does he warn you are exchanging?
item.answer: The structure comes from the speech itself. Samara says the natural rhythm of spoken language is often used as a guide for changing weight, size, colour or alignment among lines of type, with louder or faster words set larger, bolder or in italics to correspond to stresses and lulls in actual speech; giving a voice to visual language can push words out of paragraphs or force columns into relationships where the natural logic of the writing creates a visual order. His own example is a book of dialogue in which each character's voice is coded typographically and the columns are deconstructed by the quality of the speech — falling apart, becoming confused, interrupting each other. The exchange he names is explicit: breaking phrases and words apart in running text calls attention to the individual parts of speech and the presumed reading order may begin to change, which he says would generally interfere with reading; it is warranted only where the resulting ambiguity is appropriate to the content. A caption states the same trade in stronger terms — the verbal structure is brought into focus while the visual clarity is decreased.
item.support: "Verbal and Editorial Deconstruction": speech rhythm guiding weight, size, colour and alignment; the dialogue book with typographically coded voices; the concession that fragmenting running text generally interferes with reading and is warranted where the ambiguity suits the content; the caption stating that verbal structure comes into focus as visual clarity decreases.
confounders: treating the typographic variation as decoration or emphasis rather than as the structure itself
assuming Samara considers the reading cost negligible — he concedes it twice
importing a modern accessibility argument as though it were his; he does not make one
